method: COMPILED FROM 2 SOURCES. S1: QUOTED from Obeid R, Andrès E, Češka R, et al. (international Delphi panel; funded by Wörwag Pharma), Journal of Clinical Medicine (MDPI) 'Diagnosis, Treatment and Long-Term Management of Vitamin B12 Deficiency in Adults: A Delphi Expert Consensus' (published 10 April 2024), 22 claims; LICENCE: CC BY 4.0 (read at Europe PMC fullTextXML <license> element for PMC11050313). S2: PARAPHRASED AND HASH-ANCHORED from Bedz D, Forsyth C, Australian Prescriber 2026;49:55-60 (doi 10.18773/austprescr.2026.012) 'Vitamin B12 deficiency: testing and treatment' (7 April 2026 (finalised 17 February 2026)), 11 claims; LICENCE: CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 (read at Creative Commons badge and link on the article page). Verify each source separately: verify.py --source <file> --only-source S<n>. Edition 2.0 keeps every edition 1.0 claim and quote (S1, the 2024 Delphi consensus) unchanged and adds S2, a 2026 Australian Prescriber review (peer reviewed, not a guideline), for Australian testing indications, test choice, MBS rules, lifelong intramuscular replacement and monitoring. S2's tables (risk factors, clinical features, test interpretation and the treatment and dose table) and Figure 1 were stripped. The Delphi consensus statements themselves are in Tables 1 and 2, which were stripped; claims are anchored to the Results and Discussion text. The study was funded by Wörwag Pharma (a B12 manufacturer). Table rows appended with pmc_text.py --append-tables (2026-09-24); claims from S1 Table 2 (the treatment, prophylaxis and long-term consensus statements, with agreement levels). S1 Table 1 (diagnosis statements) has merged cells and was not extracted; S2 is not a PMC source, so its tables stay stripped.

claims.claim: **Symptoms are varied and mostly nonspecific**, and patients usually present in primary care. Neurological involvement affects about 30-50%; nervous-system and mental symptoms are the commonest and the hardest to link to B12.
claims.source_text: The signs and symptoms of deficiency are variable and mostly nonspecific. Patients often seek help in primary medical care. … Approximately 30-50% of patients with vitamin B12 deficiency have some degree of neurological involvement … The panelists agreed that symptoms related to the peripheral and central nervous systems are the most common symptoms in patients with clinically manifested vitamin B12 deficiency (Figure S3). At the same time, it was agreed that symptoms affecting the central nervous system (mental function and neurological function), followed by those affecting the peripheral nervous system, are the most difficult symptoms to link to B12 deficiency
claims.locator: Obeid R, Andrès E, Češka R, et al. (international Delphi panel; funded by Wörwag Pharma), Journal of Clinical Medicine (MDPI), 'Diagnosis, Treatment and Long-Term Management of Vitamin B12 Deficiency in Adults: A Delphi Expert Consensus', published 10 April 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11050313/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **A normal blood count does not exclude it:** macrocytic anaemia does not track the presence or severity of neurological symptoms.
claims.source_text: Macrocytic anemia is not related to the presence or absence of neurological symptoms or their severity
claims.locator: Obeid R, Andrès E, Češka R, et al. (international Delphi panel; funded by Wörwag Pharma), Journal of Clinical Medicine (MDPI), 'Diagnosis, Treatment and Long-Term Management of Vitamin B12 Deficiency in Adults: A Delphi Expert Consensus', published 10 April 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11050313/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Malabsorption is the main cause in adults**: pernicious anaemia, atrophic gastritis and other gut disease. Other risks include older age (food-cobalamin malabsorption), Crohn's and coeliac disease, H. pylori, gastric surgery and long-term PPIs.
claims.source_text: Malabsorption of vitamin B12 is the main cause of clinically manifested vitamin B12 deficiency among adults. Pernicious anemia (lack of intrinsic factor or antibodies against intrinsic factor), atrophic gastritis, and other gastroenteric diseases can cause B12 malabsorption. … Lowered serum vitamin B12 has been reported in people with atrophic gastritis [,], Crohn's disease [,], celiac disease [], infection with H. pylori [], gastric surgeries [,], and chronic treatment with proton pump inhibitors
claims.locator: Obeid R, Andrès E, Češka R, et al. (international Delphi panel; funded by Wörwag Pharma), Journal of Clinical Medicine (MDPI), 'Diagnosis, Treatment and Long-Term Management of Vitamin B12 Deficiency in Adults: A Delphi Expert Consensus', published 10 April 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11050313/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Metformin lowers B12 from as early as 3 months** and is linked to more neuropathy. Up to 70% of patients after gastrectomy become deficient within 12-24 months without supplements.
claims.source_text: The use of the glucose-lowering drug metformin is causally related to lowered serum concentrations of vitamin B12 [,]. The effect has been shown as early as 3 months after starting the drug … Up to 70% of patients who undergo gastrectomy may develop vitamin B12 deficiency 12-24 months after surgery if not supplemented with the vitamin
claims.locator: Obeid R, Andrès E, Češka R, et al. (international Delphi panel; funded by Wörwag Pharma), Journal of Clinical Medicine (MDPI), 'Diagnosis, Treatment and Long-Term Management of Vitamin B12 Deficiency in Adults: A Delphi Expert Consensus', published 10 April 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11050313/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Take a targeted history:** diet low in animal foods, past illnesses, regular medicines and recreational gas use (the source says 'nitric oxide'; nitrous oxide is the recognised cause).
claims.source_text: doctors need to inquire whether the person adheres to a diet that is low in foods from animal sources and should ask the person about disease history, regular use of certain medications, and recreational use of nitric oxide.
claims.locator: Obeid R, Andrès E, Češka R, et al. (international Delphi panel; funded by Wörwag Pharma), Journal of Clinical Medicine (MDPI), 'Diagnosis, Treatment and Long-Term Management of Vitamin B12 Deficiency in Adults: A Delphi Expert Consensus', published 10 April 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11050313/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **In Australia, 5.2–6.3% of people over 50 are deficient,** and people of refugee background from Afghanistan, Bhutan, Iran, Iraq or Sudan are at particular risk (20–30%). In severe cases the spinal cord can be damaged (subacute combined degeneration), and this may be permanent even once B12 is restored.
claims.locator: Bedz D, Forsyth C, Australian Prescriber 2026;49:55-60 (doi 10.18773/austprescr.2026.012), 'Vitamin B12 deficiency: testing and treatment', 7 April 2026 (finalised 17 February 2026), https://australianprescriber.tg.org.au/articles/vitamin-B12-deficiency-testing-and-treatment.html, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Serum B12 below 148 pmol/L suggests frank deficiency; 148-220 (or 260) pmol/L suggests mild deficiency.** But 30-40% of people with B12-related symptoms have a normal serum B12.
claims.source_text: However, 30-40% of people with neurological or hematological symptoms related to B12 deficiency may have normal vitamin B12 concentrations [,]. Serum vitamin B12 concentrations below 148 pmol/L (or 156 pmol/L in certain studies) are commonly considered to suggest a frank deficiency [,]. Serum B12 concentrations between 148 and 220 pmol/L or 260 pmol/L are often considered to indicate mild deficiency
claims.locator: Obeid R, Andrès E, Češka R, et al. (international Delphi panel; funded by Wörwag Pharma), Journal of Clinical Medicine (MDPI), 'Diagnosis, Treatment and Long-Term Management of Vitamin B12 Deficiency in Adults: A Delphi Expert Consensus', published 10 April 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11050313/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **The GP can start with history, examination, a full blood count and serum B12**, adding advanced markers (for example intrinsic factor antibodies with gut symptoms) when indicated, then begin treatment after the preliminary work-up.
claims.source_text: In people with symptoms suggesting vitamin B12 deficiency, the general practitioner can collect information on medical history, perform physical examinations, and perform basic laboratory tests such as full blood cell count and serum B12 concentration. Advanced clinical and laboratory markers can be ordered if there are indications (e.g., intrinsic factor antibodies in cases of gastrointestinal symptoms). After the preliminary workup, treatment with B12 can start.
claims.locator: Obeid R, Andrès E, Češka R, et al. (international Delphi panel; funded by Wörwag Pharma), Journal of Clinical Medicine (MDPI), 'Diagnosis, Treatment and Long-Term Management of Vitamin B12 Deficiency in Adults: A Delphi Expert Consensus', published 10 April 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11050313/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Methylmalonic acid and homocysteine help** to confirm deficiency and to guide treatment, and can clarify intracellular B12 status when serum B12 is unexpectedly high.
claims.source_text: there is agreement that metabolic biomarkers such as methylmalonic acid and homocysteine can be useful in guiding the diagnosis of vitamin B12 deficiency and optimizing and monitoring treatment with vitamin B12 … In this case, the concentrations of methylmalonic acid or homocysteine can provide clues on intracellular vitamin B12 status.
claims.locator: Obeid R, Andrès E, Češka R, et al. (international Delphi panel; funded by Wörwag Pharma), Journal of Clinical Medicine (MDPI), 'Diagnosis, Treatment and Long-Term Management of Vitamin B12 Deficiency in Adults: A Delphi Expert Consensus', published 10 April 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11050313/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Suspect malabsorption** with autoimmune disease, previous gastric surgery, a family history of pernicious anaemia, or positive intrinsic factor or parietal cell antibodies. Check folate and iron too.
claims.source_text: There is agreement that the malabsorption of vitamin B12 can be suspected in people with autoimmune disorders, in patients who have had gastric surgery, in people with a family history of pernicious anemia or with positive test results for serum antibodies against intrinsic factor or parietal cells. Moreover, assessing folate and iron statuses can aid in the differential diagnosis of vitamin B12 deficiency
claims.locator: Obeid R, Andrès E, Češka R, et al. (international Delphi panel; funded by Wörwag Pharma), Journal of Clinical Medicine (MDPI), 'Diagnosis, Treatment and Long-Term Management of Vitamin B12 Deficiency in Adults: A Delphi Expert Consensus', published 10 April 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11050313/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **A high serum B12 with a deficiency picture** may reflect unreported supplements, assay interference, renal or liver disease, or malignancy.
claims.source_text: High concentrations of vitamin B12 may be due to underreporting supplement use, autoimmune disorders interfering with the B12 assay, or underlying renal or liver diseases. In addition, some malignancies cause high circulating levels of vitamin B12
claims.locator: Obeid R, Andrès E, Češka R, et al. (international Delphi panel; funded by Wörwag Pharma), Journal of Clinical Medicine (MDPI), 'Diagnosis, Treatment and Long-Term Management of Vitamin B12 Deficiency in Adults: A Delphi Expert Consensus', published 10 April 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11050313/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **When to test (Australia):** only with a reasonable clinical suspicion from risk factors or findings; to explain a blood count or film abnormality (macrocytic anaemia, pancytopenia, hypersegmented neutrophils); with unexplained neurological or psychiatric symptoms even without anaemia; and reasonably in older adults being worked up for cognitive decline.
claims.locator: Bedz D, Forsyth C, Australian Prescriber 2026;49:55-60 (doi 10.18773/austprescr.2026.012), 'Vitamin B12 deficiency: testing and treatment', 7 April 2026 (finalised 17 February 2026), https://australianprescriber.tg.org.au/articles/vitamin-B12-deficiency-testing-and-treatment.html, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Do not test** people without symptoms or risk factors, the general population, people already on B12 (unless checking adherence or suspected malabsorption), or anyone with a normal result in the past 12 months unless their condition has changed. Medicare rebates each B12, active B12, methylmalonic acid and homocysteine test only once every 11 months, with a separate item for patients needing more frequent tests.
claims.locator: Bedz D, Forsyth C, Australian Prescriber 2026;49:55-60 (doi 10.18773/austprescr.2026.012), 'Vitamin B12 deficiency: testing and treatment', 7 April 2026 (finalised 17 February 2026), https://australianprescriber.tg.org.au/articles/vitamin-B12-deficiency-testing-and-treatment.html, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Which test:** total serum B12 first (cheapest); a low value confirms deficiency with no further testing. In pregnancy, and when haptocorrin is low (pregnancy, oestrogen-containing drugs), use active B12 (holotranscobalamin). Total B12 can be falsely normal or high with inflammation, myeloproliferative neoplasms, liver disease or anti-intrinsic factor antibody interference.
claims.locator: Bedz D, Forsyth C, Australian Prescriber 2026;49:55-60 (doi 10.18773/austprescr.2026.012), 'Vitamin B12 deficiency: testing and treatment', 7 April 2026 (finalised 17 February 2026), https://australianprescriber.tg.org.au/articles/vitamin-B12-deficiency-testing-and-treatment.html, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Normal methylmalonic acid and homocysteine exclude deficiency;** raised values are not specific: homocysteine rises with folate or B6 deficiency, CKD, hypothyroidism and MTHFR variants, and methylmalonic acid with CKD, though it is usually normal in folate deficiency.
claims.locator: Bedz D, Forsyth C, Australian Prescriber 2026;49:55-60 (doi 10.18773/austprescr.2026.012), 'Vitamin B12 deficiency: testing and treatment', 7 April 2026 (finalised 17 February 2026), https://australianprescriber.tg.org.au/articles/vitamin-B12-deficiency-testing-and-treatment.html, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Suspected nitrous oxide use: test homocysteine or methylmalonic acid first,** because nitrous oxide inactivates B12 and total and active B12 can look normal despite tissue deficiency.
claims.locator: Bedz D, Forsyth C, Australian Prescriber 2026;49:55-60 (doi 10.18773/austprescr.2026.012), 'Vitamin B12 deficiency: testing and treatment', 7 April 2026 (finalised 17 February 2026), https://australianprescriber.tg.org.au/articles/vitamin-B12-deficiency-testing-and-treatment.html, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Suspect autoimmune gastritis** in unexplained deficiency, especially with upper GI symptoms or other autoimmune disease: test anti-intrinsic factor antibodies; if negative, consider parietal cell antibodies, gastrin and gastroscopy. If the cause is still unknown, test for coeliac disease and *H. pylori*.
claims.locator: Bedz D, Forsyth C, Australian Prescriber 2026;49:55-60 (doi 10.18773/austprescr.2026.012), 'Vitamin B12 deficiency: testing and treatment', 7 April 2026 (finalised 17 February 2026), https://australianprescriber.tg.org.au/articles/vitamin-B12-deficiency-testing-and-treatment.html, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **With suspected severe deficiency, start treatment without delay**, but draw blood for B12 markers first.
claims.source_text: in patients with clinically suspected severe B12 deficiency, there must not be any delay in initiating appropriate B12 treatment. Serum specimens for measuring vitamin B12 marker(s) should be collected prior to treatment.
claims.locator: Obeid R, Andrès E, Češka R, et al. (international Delphi panel; funded by Wörwag Pharma), Journal of Clinical Medicine (MDPI), 'Diagnosis, Treatment and Long-Term Management of Vitamin B12 Deficiency in Adults: A Delphi Expert Consensus', published 10 April 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11050313/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Acute or severe symptoms call for parenteral B12 first**, typically injections for several weeks initially. Prefer oral treatment where injections are contraindicated, for example on anticoagulants.
claims.source_text: it was agreed that the acuity and severity of the symptoms of vitamin B12 deficiency necessitate prioritizing treatment with parenteral vitamin B12. Contraindications to parenteral use, such as in people receiving anticoagulant medication, need to be taken into consideration, and oral supplementation may be preferred in those cases. … In people with severe signs and symptoms, the use of injectable forms of vitamin B12 for several weeks is acknowledged, at least in the initial treatment phase.
claims.locator: Obeid R, Andrès E, Češka R, et al. (international Delphi panel; funded by Wörwag Pharma), Journal of Clinical Medicine (MDPI), 'Diagnosis, Treatment and Long-Term Management of Vitamin B12 Deficiency in Adults: A Delphi Expert Consensus', published 10 April 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11050313/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Dose:** there is no gold standard. For manifest deficiency or malabsorption, 1000-2000 µg/day orally or 1000 µg IM (for example daily, then weekly, then monthly for maintenance). In subacute combined degeneration, larger, more frequent doses work better.
claims.source_text: There is currently no gold standard for choosing the dose and route of B12 administration. Various protocols have been used successfully. In general, whenever B12 deficiency is clinically manifested or the patient cannot absorb B12, therapeutic doses between 1000 µg/day and 2000 µg/day orally or 1000 µg i.m. (e.g., daily, then weekly, then monthly for maintenance treatment) can be used. … The clinical response to B12 treatment in SCD patients is expected to be better when large doses of B12 are administered more frequently than when B12 is administered less frequently
claims.locator: Obeid R, Andrès E, Češka R, et al. (international Delphi panel; funded by Wörwag Pharma), Journal of Clinical Medicine (MDPI), 'Diagnosis, Treatment and Long-Term Management of Vitamin B12 Deficiency in Adults: A Delphi Expert Consensus', published 10 April 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11050313/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Maintenance in malabsorption:** 1000-1500 µg/day orally or 1000 µg IM every 1-3 months keeps B12 in range. Low-dose supplements (3-6 µg/day) or 1000 µg orally once a week will not correct it. High-dose oral and IM are likely equivalent.
claims.source_text: In people with vitamin B12 malabsorption, 1000-1500 µg/day of oral vitamin B12 [,] or 1000 µg i.m. B12 every 1-3 months is adequate as a maintenance treatment to keep serum B12 concentrations within the reference range [,]. Lowered serum concentrations of vitamin B12 are unlikely to be corrected by using 3-6 µg/day B12 from food supplements or high oral B12 (1000 µg) provided once weekly [,]. High dose oral and i.m. protocols are likely to be equivalent in correcting serum B12 concentrations
claims.locator: Obeid R, Andrès E, Češka R, et al. (international Delphi panel; funded by Wörwag Pharma), Journal of Clinical Medicine (MDPI), 'Diagnosis, Treatment and Long-Term Management of Vitamin B12 Deficiency in Adults: A Delphi Expert Consensus', published 10 April 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11050313/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Long-term route should balance treatment goals with patient preference.** If treatment fails, reconsider the diagnosis and the dose, and consider parenteral B12, especially after oral treatment or if serum B12 has not normalised.
claims.source_text: The decision on the route of administration during long-term treatment needs to balance treatment goals and patient preference. If vitamin B12 treatment failed to alleviate the patient's symptoms, the panelists agreed that doctors should consider alternative conditions that may explain the symptoms and should reevaluate the appropriateness of the dose of B12 therapy. In nonresponsive cases, doctors can consider using parenteral B12, especially if oral B12 treatment has been used in the past or when serum vitamin B12 is not normalized
claims.locator: Obeid R, Andrès E, Češka R, et al. (international Delphi panel; funded by Wörwag Pharma), Journal of Clinical Medicine (MDPI), 'Diagnosis, Treatment and Long-Term Management of Vitamin B12 Deficiency in Adults: A Delphi Expert Consensus', published 10 April 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11050313/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Australian advice: lifelong intramuscular B12 when the cause is pernicious anaemia, autoimmune gastritis, a total gastrectomy or resection of the terminal ileum,** because absorption is permanently impaired and oral B12 is unreliable even at high doses. This is more cautious than S1, which treats high-dose oral B12 as likely equivalent in malabsorption; S2 notes a 2024 meta-analysis finding oral and sublingual B12 as effective as injections but calls for better trials.
claims.locator: Bedz D, Forsyth C, Australian Prescriber 2026;49:55-60 (doi 10.18773/austprescr.2026.012), 'Vitamin B12 deficiency: testing and treatment', 7 April 2026 (finalised 17 February 2026), https://australianprescriber.tg.org.au/articles/vitamin-B12-deficiency-testing-and-treatment.html, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Indeterminate levels with risk factors:** a trial of B12 can be considered after careful assessment, with review and deprescribing where appropriate. Choose route, dose and duration by cause, severity, cost and preference.
claims.locator: Bedz D, Forsyth C, Australian Prescriber 2026;49:55-60 (doi 10.18773/austprescr.2026.012), 'Vitamin B12 deficiency: testing and treatment', 7 April 2026 (finalised 17 February 2026), https://australianprescriber.tg.org.au/articles/vitamin-B12-deficiency-testing-and-treatment.html, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Judge response mainly on symptoms.** No improvement after 4-8 weeks for anaemia or 6-12 months for neurological signs suggests another cause or an inadequate dose or route. A slow early response should not by itself stop treatment.
claims.source_text: In general, determining the severity of B12 deficiency and the response to treatment primarily relies on evaluating clinical symptoms. … The lack of clinical improvement after 4-8 weeks for anemia and after 6-12 months for neurological signs could suggest that the symptoms are not due to B12 deficiency or that the dose of vitamin B12 or the route of administration needs to be adjusted to the severity of symptoms. … An insufficient clinical response to B12 treatment during the first weeks of therapy should not routinely lead to the discontinuation of treatment.
claims.locator: Obeid R, Andrès E, Češka R, et al. (international Delphi panel; funded by Wörwag Pharma), Journal of Clinical Medicine (MDPI), 'Diagnosis, Treatment and Long-Term Management of Vitamin B12 Deficiency in Adults: A Delphi Expert Consensus', published 10 April 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11050313/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Recovery can be incomplete:** up to 25% keep severe neurological symptoms despite normal blood markers, and sensory symptoms can take up to one year to settle. Longer, more severe deficiency before treatment means slower and less complete recovery.
claims.source_text: Up to 25% of patients have been reported to retain severe neurological symptoms despite the normalization of blood marker levels … Symptoms of neuropathy mostly improve within several months but may take up to one year for sensory symptoms to resolve after the start of B12 therapy … The duration and severity of pretreatment deficiency symptoms have a clear impact on the time course and degree of recovery after starting B12 therapy [,], thus emphasizing the importance of early identification and prevention.
claims.locator: Obeid R, Andrès E, Češka R, et al. (international Delphi panel; funded by Wörwag Pharma), Journal of Clinical Medicine (MDPI), 'Diagnosis, Treatment and Long-Term Management of Vitamin B12 Deficiency in Adults: A Delphi Expert Consensus', published 10 April 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11050313/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Recheck serum B12 case by case** (new symptoms, adherence or absorption of oral therapy); it tracks clinical response poorly. Periodic B12 checks can help find at-risk people such as long-term metformin users.
claims.source_text: measuring serum B12 concentrations to monitor B12 treatment should be decided on a case-by-case basis (for example, when people show new symptoms, to check compliance with oral treatment, and to check whether B12 was absorbed after oral administration). … The panelists agreed that the periodic measurement of serum concentrations of vitamin B12 can be helpful in identifying people at risk of deficiency, such as people receiving long-term metformin treatment.
claims.locator: Obeid R, Andrès E, Češka R, et al. (international Delphi panel; funded by Wörwag Pharma), Journal of Clinical Medicine (MDPI), 'Diagnosis, Treatment and Long-Term Management of Vitamin B12 Deficiency in Adults: A Delphi Expert Consensus', published 10 April 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11050313/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Give prophylactic B12** with atrophic gastritis, after bariatric surgery, with illnesses or medicines that cause deficiency, and with little or no animal food. Women with previous or at-risk deficiency should take it from before pregnancy to the end of breastfeeding.
claims.source_text: The prophylactic use of vitamin B12 was regarded as necessary for people diagnosed with atrophic gastritis, those with previous bariatric surgery, people at risk of B12 deficiency due to illnesses or medications, people with low or no consumption of animal source foods, and people ever diagnosed with vitamin B12 deficiency when they decided to become pregnant … prophylactic B12 supplementation should be used from prepregnancy until the end of the lactation period in women with previously diagnosed B12 deficiency or who are at risk of vitamin B12 deficiency due for instance to low dietary intake of B12.
claims.locator: Obeid R, Andrès E, Češka R, et al. (international Delphi panel; funded by Wörwag Pharma), Journal of Clinical Medicine (MDPI), 'Diagnosis, Treatment and Long-Term Management of Vitamin B12 Deficiency in Adults: A Delphi Expert Consensus', published 10 April 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11050313/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Consensus statements on long-term B12 (S1 Table 2):** people who have had bariatric surgery should have long-term B12 therapy or prophylaxis (agreement 0.90); deficiency in pregnancy, breastfeeding and infancy must be found and treated as early as possible because of its serious effects on fetal and infant development (0.89); and women with past deficiency or a diet low in animal foods should take prophylaxis from before pregnancy to the end of breastfeeding (0.92).
claims.source_text: Question: People who underwent bariatric surgery in the past should receive B12 therapy or prophylactic B12 supplementation for long-term. · n (Panelists) 1: 41 · Mean (95% CI) 2: 0.90 (0.77-0.97) … [Table 2 row 16] 5. · Question: B12 deficiency during pregnancy, lactation and in infancy needs to be detected and treated as early as possible because of the serious effects of B12 deficiency on fetal and infant development. · n (Panelists) 1: 38 · Mean (95% CI) 2: 0.89 (0.75-0.97) [Table 2 row 17] 6. · Question: Women with a previously diagnosed B12 deficiency or dietary restriction of animal foods should take prophylactic B12 supplementation from pre-pregnancy to the end of the lactation period. · n (Panelists) 1: 38 · Mean (95% CI) 2: 0.92 (0.79-0.98)
claims.locator: Obeid R, Andrès E, Češka R, et al. (international Delphi panel; funded by Wörwag Pharma), Journal of Clinical Medicine (MDPI), 'Diagnosis, Treatment and Long-Term Management of Vitamin B12 Deficiency in Adults: A Delphi Expert Consensus', published 10 April 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11050313/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **No B12 form is proven better (S1 Table 2):** it is unclear whether the available forms differ in effectiveness or safety, and head-to-head trials are needed (agreement 0.88, 42 panellists).
claims.source_text: [Table 2 row 1] 1. · Question: At present, it is unclear whether different forms of B12 differ in their effectiveness or safety. Clinical trials comparing the safety and effectiveness of the commercially available forms are needed. · n (Panelists) 1: 42 · Mean (95% CI) 2: 0.88 (0.74-0.96)
claims.locator: Obeid R, Andrès E, Češka R, et al. (international Delphi panel; funded by Wörwag Pharma), Journal of Clinical Medicine (MDPI), 'Diagnosis, Treatment and Long-Term Management of Vitamin B12 Deficiency in Adults: A Delphi Expert Consensus', published 10 April 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11050313/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **How strong the consensus was:** a statement passed when the lower 95% confidence bound of the share agreeing or strongly agreeing was 50% or more. The least-agreed treatment statement was preferring oral B12 when injections are contraindicated, for example by anticoagulants (0.75, 95% CI 0.57–0.89).
claims.source_text: Question: Contraindications of intramuscular injections such as concurrent anticoagulant medication can lead to prioritizing oral B12 treatment. · n (Panelists) 1: 32 · Mean (95% CI) 2: 0.75 (0.57-0.89) … [Table 2 footnote] 1 Total number of the panelists who answered each of the questions. 2 Mean percentage and the 95% confidence intervals of the panelists who considered themselves qualified to answer the question and chose "agree" or "strongly agree" to the answer. We considered that a consensus was reached when the lower bound of the 95%confidence intervals is 50% or higher.
claims.locator: Obeid R, Andrès E, Češka R, et al. claims.claim: **Expected recovery (S2):** symptoms usually start improving within 2 weeks; reticulocytes rise in 3–5 days, haemoglobin normalises in 4–8 weeks, and neurological symptoms improve gradually over 6–12 weeks.
